title: The Haphel and Aphel

objectives.can: Recognise and parse Haphel and Aphel forms.

explanation.summary: The Haphel and the Aphel are the causative stems of Aramaic. They make a verb that means 'to cause to ...': to make known, to set up, to bring. In the Aramaic of the Bible the Haphel is the commoner by far, and it keeps a ה after the prefix of the imperfect and the participle. The Aphel has an א in the perfect, and its participle begins with מַ-.

sections.heading: What a causative stem does
body: A causative verb says that the subject makes someone else do the action or be in the state. The Peal יְדַע means 'he knew'. The Haphel הוֹדַע means 'he made known', that is, 'he caused to know'. The Peal קָם means 'he stood up'; the Haphel הֲקֵים means 'he set up'. In both cases the Haphel adds a new subject, the one who makes something happen, and the earlier subject becomes the object.

The causative of a verb that takes no object is easy to see. The Peal נְפַק 'he went out' has the causative הַנְפֵּק 'he took out'. The Peal עֲלַל 'he went in' has the causative הַנְעֵל 'he brought in'. A causative can also be the causative of a state: the verb 'be low' has the Haphel הַשְׁפֵּלְתְּ 'you humbled', as in Daniel 5:22. The stems of the same verb must be learned together.

sections.heading: The Haphel
body: The Haphel is marked by a prefix ה-, in the perfect, the infinitive and the imperative, and the first root consonant takes a short vowel with it. The perfect: הֲקֵים 'he set up', הֲקֵימְתָּ 'you set up', הֲקֵימֶת 'I set up' and הֲתִיב 'he returned'. In verbs whose first consonant is י the ה- is followed by וֹ: הוֹדַע 'he made known'. The Haphel perfect has the usual endings of the perfect, and the third person plural ends in -וּ or, in a verb with a weak last consonant, in -יו (הַיְתִיו 'they brought').

In the imperfect and the participle the Haphel keeps its ה after the prefix. This is a clear mark of the stem: יְהוֹדַע 'he will make known', יְהָקֵים 'he will set up', תְהַשְׁכַּח 'you will find' (literally 'you will cause to be found'), and, in the participle, מְהוֹדְעִין 'making known' and וּמְהָקֵים 'and setting up'. The Haphel participle has the prefix מְ- as the Pael has; the ה after it is the difference.
The Haphel infinitive has the prefix לְ- or לַ- and ה-, and in most verbs ends in -ָה: לְהַחֲוָיָה 'to declare', לְהוֹדָעָה 'to make known', לְהַשְׁנָיָה 'to change'.

sections.heading: The Aphel
body: The Aphel is the causative with an א in place of ה. The texts have only twenty-four Aphel forms, in a few verbs, but they are not hard to spot. In the perfect the prefix is א-, as in אֲקִימֵהּ 'he set it up' (Daniel 3:1; the suffix -ֵהּ is the object 'it'). The imperative begins with the same letter: אֲחֵת 'bring down!'.

The Aphel imperfect has no ה after the prefix: יְקִים 'he will set up', תְּקִים 'you will set up', וְתַחֵת 'and you will bring down'. The Aphel participle begins with מַ-, with a long or short a and no ה: מַהְלְכִין 'walking', וּמַצְלְחִין 'and prospering', מַשְׁפִּיל 'bringing low', מָרִים 'raising up'. Compare the Haphel participle, which begins מְהַ- or מְהוֹ-.

sections.heading: How the Haphel and the Aphel are used together
body: The two stems have the same causative meaning. In the Aramaic of the Bible a verb usually has one or the other, and the analysed texts label them as they appear. For the verb 'arise' both occur: the perfect is a Haphel (הֲקֵים) and the imperfect is an Aphel (יְקִים) in some forms. That is the data and not a mistake.

A look at Daniel 2:44 shows why the stem matters. The verse has the Aphel יְקִים, 'will set up', for what God does, and the Peal תְּקוּם, 'will stand', for what the kingdom does. Without the stem the two verbs, from the same root, would seem to be the same.

sections.heading: The Shaphel
body: A few verbs have a causative formed with שׁ, the Shaphel. Some grammarians connect it with verbs borrowed from other languages. The texts have it in two verbs: שֵׁיזִיב 'he delivered', מְשֵׁיזִב 'delivering', and לְשַׁכְלָלָה 'to complete'. The forms are few, and the stem is recognised by the שׁ- prefix in the place where the ה or א would stand.

misunderstandings: Do not read the ה of the Haphel as a part of the root. In the imperfect and the participle it stands between the prefix and the root: look at the root after it.
A prefix ה- does not always mean the Haphel. The Hophal, the Hithpeel and the Hithpaal also begin with ה. Check the vowels and the following letters, and the sense: a causative, not a passive.
The Aphel is not rare because the language lacks it, but because the texts have little of it: twenty-four forms. Do not expect an Aphel in every verse.
A Haphel and a Peal of the same verb are not the same verb. The Haphel adds the one who causes the action, so it takes an extra object.

deeper.heading: Why two causative stems
body: Grammarians connect the ה- of the Haphel with an older Aramaic causative, and the א- of the Aphel with a development that became standard in later Aramaic. The Aramaic of the Bible contains both, and it is common to find the Haphel in the perfect and the Aphel in other forms of the same verb. The explanation is a matter of the history of the language, and the learner can leave it at that.

examples.analysis: Three Haphel forms. וְהַדֶּקֶת (11) is a Haphel perfect, third person feminine singular: the stone 'broke in pieces' (it caused them to be shattered). הוֹדַע (19) is a Haphel perfect, third person masculine singular, 'made known': God is the subject. וּמְהֵימַן (28) is a Haphel participle, passive in sense: 'trustworthy'. Notice that the same root יְדַע is Peal in the sense 'know' elsewhere.

examples.analysis: יְקִים (4) is an Aphel imperfect, third person masculine singular: 'God of heaven will set up a kingdom'. It has no ה- after the prefix. תְּקוּם (23) is the Peal imperfect, third person feminine singular, of the same root: the kingdom 'will stand'. The causative and its Peal are in one verse.

examples.analysis: מָרִים (28) and מַשְׁפִּיל (33) are Aphel participles, masculine singular absolute, with the prefix מ- and a vowel a. They mean 'raising up' and 'bringing low', and they describe the king's power. They are the last of a series of clauses in which the verb 'to be' is paired with a participle, a construction taught in A4.1.3.
